## Statement

Assume AC. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on an arbitrary measurable space $(X,\mathcal F)$, with invariant probability $\pi$, finite measurable $M:X\to[0,\infty)$ and $0<r<1$ satisfying
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in X,\ n\ge1).$$
Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be finite measurable. For each specified initial law $\mu$, there are a nonempty standard-Borel space $S$, a probability kernel $T$ on $S$, an invariant probability $\widehat\pi$, an initial probability $\widehat\mu$, and finite measurable functions $\varphi:S\to\mathbb R$ and $\widehat M:S\to[0,\infty)$ such that
$$\|T^n(z,\cdot)-\widehat\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\widehat M(z)r^n\quad(z\in S,\ n\ge1).$$
The complete observation path $(f(X_n))_{n\ge0}$ of a $\mu$-started $P$-chain has the same law as $(\varphi(Y_n))_{n\ge0}$ of a $\widehat\mu$-started $T$-chain. The corresponding stationary observation paths also have the same law, and $\widehat\pi(|\varphi|^a)=\pi(|f|^a)$ for every $a>0$, with infinity allowed. The factor may depend on $\mu$.

Moreover, any joint law of that observation path with a random element of a standard-Borel space can be lifted to an extension preserving the entire original chain probability space and process.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and the objects and geometric bound in the Statement.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC supplies the inherited coding, factorization, disintegration and extension conventions.

[F1] [[lem-countably-generated-kernel-stable-sub-sigma-field]]: a real observable lies in a countably generated kernel-stable sub-sigma-field, with restricted iterates and invariant law.

[F2] [[thm-standard-borel-spaces-admit-bimeasurable-real-codings]], [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]], and [[lem-real-line-is-standard-borel]]: real finite tuples and standard-Borel spaces have Borel real codings.

[F3] [[thm-doob-dynkin-lemma]]: a real or extended-real function measurable for the sigma-field of a real code factors through a Borel function of that code.

[F4] [[thm-disintegration-of-a-joint-law-on-standard-borel-spaces]]: standard-Borel joint laws have measurable conditional probability kernels, unique outside a single null set.

[F5] [[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]]: probability measures agreeing on a generating algebra agree everywhere.

[F6] [[thm-markov-property-for-bounded-future-path-functionals]]: the original Markov conditional identities hold, and bounded future-observation expectations are measurable.

[F7] [[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]]: supplied measurable probability kernels extend an initial probability space while preserving its marginal.

[F8] [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]] and [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]: nonnegative limits and probability-kernel integrals have their usual measurability and integral identities.

[F9] [[def-standard-borel-space]] and [[cor-countable-products-and-g-delta-subspaces-of-polish-spaces-are-polish]]: Borel subspaces of Polish presentations are standard Borel, and countable products of Polish spaces are Polish under the assumed choice convention.

[F10] [[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]] and [[def-iterated-transition-kernels]]: invariance is $\pi P=\pi$, and iterates are successive kernel integrations.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement and AC [A1].

1.1 Define
$$\lambda=\tfrac12\pi+\tfrac12\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-k-1}\mu P^k.$$
This is a probability by [F8], $\pi,\mu\ll\lambda$, and $\lambda P\ll\lambda$: if $\lambda(A)=0$, then $\pi(A)=0$ and $\mu P^k(A)=0$ for every $k$, which also makes $\lambda P(A)=0$. Thus $\lambda P^j\ll\lambda$ for every $j$. Apply [F2] to code the pair $(f,M)$ into one real observable, and apply [F1] to it. The resulting countably generated $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ is kernel-stable and contains both $f$ and $M$, since the coding has a Borel inverse. [A1, F1, F2, F8, F10, construct, given]

1.2 Enumerate generators $A_j$ of $\mathcal G$ and set $c(x)=\sum_{j\ge1}2\cdot3^{-j}1_{A_j}(x)$, taking values in the closed Cantor subset $C$ of $[0,1]$. Its coordinate digits recover every $A_j$, so $\sigma(c)=\mathcal G$. The target $C$ is standard Borel by [F9]; no Borel-image assertion about $c(X)$ is needed. By [F3], write $f=\varphi_0\circ c$ and $M=m_0\circ c$ for Borel extended-real functions on $C$. Put $\lambda_c=c_*\lambda$, $\pi_c=c_*\pi$ and $\mu_c=c_*\mu$. [A1, F3, F9, step 1.1, construct]

2.1 Push the probability $\lambda(dx)P(x,dy)$ to $(c(x),c(y))\in C^2$ and disintegrate by [F4], obtaining a Borel kernel $T:C\to C$. For each $B$ in a fixed countable generating algebra of $C$, kernel stability and [F3] factor $P(x,c^{-1}B)$ through $c(x)$. Its value is the conditional mean of $1_B(c(X_1))$ given $c(X_0)$ under this reference joint law. Hence $T(c(x),B)=P(x,c^{-1}B)$ for $\lambda$-almost every $x$. Intersect over the countable algebra and apply [F5] to obtain equality of these probability measures simultaneously on every Borel $B$, on one $\lambda$-full set. In particular $\lambda_cT=c_*(\lambda P)\ll\lambda_c$, and $\pi_cT=\pi_c$ because $\pi\ll\lambda$ and $\pi P=\pi$. [A1, F3, F4, F5, F7, F8, F10, step 1.1, step 1.2]

2.2 Iterating that kernel equality gives $T^n(c(x),\cdot)=c_*P^n(x,\cdot)$ for $\lambda$-almost every $x$, simultaneously for all $n\ge0$. At the induction step, $P(x,\cdot)$ avoids the preceding $\lambda$-null exceptional set for $\lambda$-almost every $x$, since $\lambda P\ll\lambda$; integration of a nonnegative Borel function of $c$ agrees under the two one-step measures by simple approximation and [F8]. The geometric hypothesis therefore implies $\|T^n(z,\cdot)-\pi_c\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le m_0(z)r^n$ for $\lambda_c$-almost every $z$, simultaneously for $n\ge1$. [F8, F10, step 1.1, step 2.1, given]

2.3 On $C$ the total-variation supremum can be taken over its fixed countable generating algebra. Indeed, for any two probabilities, every Borel set is approximable in symmetric-difference measure by that algebra under their finite sum: the approximable sets form a sigma-field, using complements and first approximating a countable union by a finite union. Its probability difference is approximated too. Thus the supremum over the algebra equals the full supremum and is measurable as a function of the starting point. Let $B_0$ be the Borel set where all the bounds in step 2.2 hold and $\varphi_0,m_0$ are finite with $m_0\ge0$. It is $\lambda_c$-full by step 1.2 and the finiteness of $f,M$. Define $B_{j+1}=B_j\cap\{z:T(z,B_j)=1\}$ and $S=\bigcap_{j\ge0}B_j$. Absolute continuity $\lambda_cT\ll\lambda_c$ makes every $B_j$ full. If $z\in S$, continuity from above gives $T(z,S)=1$. Thus $S$ is nonempty, Borel and absorbing. [F8, F9, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, construct]

2.4 Restrict $T$ to $S$, and set $\widehat\pi=\pi_c|_S$, $\widehat\mu=\mu_c|_S$, $\varphi=\varphi_0|_S$ and $\widehat M=m_0|_S$. These are probabilities and finite functions because $\pi_c,\mu_c\ll\lambda_c$. Absorption preserves $\widehat\pi T=\widehat\pi$. By the definition of $B_0$ the geometric bound now holds for every state in $S$, with the original rate $r$. Its total variation on $S$ is the same as on $C$ for measures supported on $S$. [F9, F10, step 2.1, step 2.3, construct]

3.1 For an original chain with initial law $\mu$, every $X_k$ has law $\mu P^k\ll\lambda$. Thus step 2.1 and [F6], followed by conditioning on the coded past, show that $c(X_k)$ is a $T$-chain. Countably many time and algebra tests suffice; [F5] and bounded approximation extend them to every bounded Borel test. The code chain remains in $S$ almost surely and $f(X_k)=\varphi(c(X_k))$ simultaneously for every $k$. The same argument applies with initial law $\pi$. This proves the complete initial and stationary observation-path equalities and, by pushforward integration, every stated stationary moment identity. [F3, F5, F6, F8, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.4]

3.2 A countable path space over a standard-Borel space is standard Borel: code its coordinates by [F2] into a Borel subset $D$ of $[0,1]$; then $D^{\mathbb N_0}$ is Borel in the Polish cube $[0,1]^{\mathbb N_0}$ by a countable intersection of coordinate tests, using [F9]. In particular the real observation-path space is standard Borel. Disintegrate any specified joint law of this path and a standard-Borel auxiliary random element conditional on the path by [F4]. Evaluate that kernel at the actual original observation path and use [F7] to extend the original probability space. Its original marginal is unchanged, and the observation/auxiliary joint law is exactly the specified law. This proves the final lifting assertion without any conditional kernel on the original arbitrary state space. [A1, F2, F4, F7, F9, step 3.1] ∎

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $P$ be a probability kernel on an arbitrary measurable space $(X,\mathcal F)$, and let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. There is a countably generated sub-sigma-field $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ such that $f$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable and $P$, restricted to events in $\mathcal G$, is a probability kernel $P_{\mathcal G}$ on $(X,\mathcal G)$. For every $n\ge0$, $x\in X$, and $B\in\mathcal G$,
$$P_{\mathcal G}^n(x,B)=P^n(x,B).$$
If $\pi$ is invariant for $P$, then $\pi|_{\mathcal G}$ is invariant for $P_{\mathcal G}$.
Assume AC. Every standard-Borel space $(E,\mathcal S)$ is measurably isomorphic to a Borel subset of $[0,1]$, including $E=\varnothing$.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

The measurable space $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ with its usual
topology is standard Borel.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ and $g : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$. Then $g$ is
$\sigma(f)$-measurable if and only if there is a Borel measurable function
$h : \mathbb{R} \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ such that

$$g = h \circ f.$$

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Assume Choice. Let $X$ be a $K$-chain and let
$H:E^{\mathbb N_0}\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and product-measurable. Then
$$h(x):=\mathbb E_x[H(X_0,X_1,\ldots)]$$ is $\mathcal E$-measurable and, for every $n\ge0$, $$ \mathbb E[H(X_n,X_{n+1},\ldots)\mid\mathcal F_n]=h(X_n)\quad\text{a.s.} $$

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. A countable product of Polish spaces is Polish, and every $G_\delta$ subspace of a Polish space is Polish.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

For a probability kernel $K$ on $(E,\mathcal E)$, let $I$ be the identity
kernel $I(x,A)=1_A(x)$ and define
$$ K^0:=I,\qquad K^{n+1}:=K^nK, $$ where composition is in chronological order: $$ K^{n+1}(x,A)=\int_E K(y,A)K^n(x,dy). $$
The identity map makes $I$ a probability kernel, including on a one-point
space. Induction using the published kernel-composition lemma shows that every
$K^n$ is a probability kernel. Associativity makes products of several copies
of $K$ unambiguous. No conditional-expectation version is selected and no form
of Choice is used.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on a nonempty standard-Borel space $(S,\mathcal S)$, with invariant probability $\pi$, finite measurable $M:S\to[0,\infty)$ and $0<r<1$ such that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in S,\ n\ge1).$$
Let $f:S\to\mathbb R$ be finite measurable, with $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi(|f|^v)<\infty$ for some $v>1$. For every initial law, on an extension preserving the given chain there are an integer $m\ge1$, an almost surely finite delay $D\in m\mathbb N$, a standard-Borel seed space $E$, iid seeds $(U_j)_{j\ge0}$, and measurable finite-word and length functions $W:E^2\to\bigsqcup_{k\ge1}S^k$ and $L:E\to m\mathbb N$ with the following properties.

Put $T_0=D$ and $T_{j+1}=T_j+L(U_j)$. Almost surely, simultaneously for all $j\ge0$,
$$\bigl(X_{T_j},\ldots,X_{T_{j+1}-1}\bigr)=W(U_j,U_{j+1}).$$
Write $L_j=L(U_j)$, $Z_j=\sum_{t=T_j}^{T_{j+1}-1}f(X_t)$, and $H_j=\sum_{t=T_j}^{T_{j+1}-1}|f(X_t)|$. Then $Z_j=z(U_j,U_{j+1})$ and $H_j=h(U_j,U_{j+1})$ for measurable functions $z,h$, and
$$\mathbb E e^{aL_0}<\infty\text{ for some }a>0,\qquad 0<\mu_L:=\mathbb EL_0<\infty,$$
$$\mathbb EZ_0=0,\qquad \mathbb EH_0^q<\infty\quad(1\le q<v).$$
For every nonnegative measurable $b:S\to[0,\infty]$ the full-tour occupation identity is
$$\mathbb E\sum_{t=T_0}^{T_1-1}b(X_t)=\mu_L\pi(b).$$
For each specified initial law, the same $m$, iid seed law, $W,L$ and post-delay tour law can be used also for the invariant initial law $\pi$; only the finite initial segment and coupling change.

In particular $(L_j-\mu_L,Z_j)$ is an adjacent-iid centered vector sequence, while the lengths themselves are iid. Full tour words or rewards are not asserted to be iid. No moment of $D$ or of the initial finite prefix is required, and the construction uses a useful multistep split chosen from $P$ rather than requiring any supplied one-step minorization to have positive stationary mass.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and the standard-Borel chain, geometric bound, invariant law, and finite centered observable in the Statement.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC supplies the inherited small-set, path-law, coding, product and disintegration conventions.

[F1] [[def-phi-irreducible-chain]] and [[lem-phi-irreducible-chain-has-small-set]]: on a countably generated irreducible state space there is a positive-measure $m$-small set, with a minorizing probability giving that set positive mass.

[F2] [[lem-geometric-split-renewal-gives-integrable-hitting-time]]: under its scalar geometric-return-probability hypothesis the explicitly specified split atom has an exponential positive return moment and finite mean.

[F3] [[thm-disintegration-of-a-joint-law-on-standard-borel-spaces]] and [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]: finite standard-Borel joint laws have measurable conditional probability kernels.

[F4] [[thm-standard-borel-spaces-admit-bimeasurable-real-codings]], [[def-standard-borel-space]], and [[cor-countable-products-and-g-delta-subspaces-of-polish-spaces-are-polish]]: standard-Borel spaces have Borel real codings; countable sequences of such coordinates and finite words are standard Borel through Borel subsets of the Polish cube.

[F5] [[cor-canonical-markov-chain-on-path-space]], [[thm-countable-product-of-probability-spaces]], and [[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]]: canonical kernel paths, iid products and extensions by specified kernels exist under AC.

[F6] [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]], [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], and [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: the kernel expectations and nonnegative sums below are measurable, and increasing limits pass through them.

[F7] [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]] and [[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]]: the indicated Holder and finite-sum $L^q$ bounds hold for $q\ge1$.

[F8] [[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]] and [[def-iterated-transition-kernels]]: $\pi P=\pi$ and iterated transitions are successive kernel integrations; consequently $\pi P^k=\pi$ for every $k$ by induction.

[F9] [[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]]: equality of probabilities or kernel identities extends from a countable generating algebra to all measurable events.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement and AC [A1].

1.1 For every $\pi$-positive measurable set $A$, the geometric bound implies $P^n(x,A)>0$ for all sufficiently large $n$, for each $x$. Thus $P$ is $\pi$-irreducible. By [F4], a standard-Borel space has a countable generating algebra, so [F1] gives $m\ge1$, $D_0$ with $\pi(D_0)>0$, a probability $\nu_0$ with $\nu_0(D_0)>0$, and $\epsilon_0>0$ such that $P^m(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon_0\nu_0$ on $D_0$. Choose an integer $K$ so $C=D_0\cap\{M\le K\}$ is positive under both $\pi$ and $\nu_0$, and restrict $\nu_0$ to $\{M\le L\}$ for a finite integer $L\ge K$, then normalize. Decrease the minorization constant to $0<\epsilon<1$. With $Q=P^m$, the resulting probability $\nu$ satisfies $Q(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon\nu$ on $C$, $\nu(M)\le L$ and $\pi(C)>0$. [A1, F1, F4, given, choose, construct]

1.2 Put $p=\epsilon\pi(C)>0$. Invariance [F8] gives $\pi\ge p\nu$. The geometric bound gives $|\nu Q^n(C)-\pi(C)|\le L(r^m)^n$ for $n\ge1$; for $n=0$ use $1$. Thus [F2] applies to this exact split. Its atom $\alpha=C\times\{1\}$ has a positive return time $\tau$ with $\mathbb E b^\tau<\infty$ for some $b>1$. The transition out of $\alpha$ draws the next skeleton state from $\nu$ independently of the previous state, and assigns its fresh flag with success probability $\epsilon1_C$. [F2, F8, step 1.1, given]

2.1 Define the substochastic failure kernel $K_0(x,dy)=Q(x,dy)-\epsilon1_C(x)\nu(dy)$, and let $a(x)$ be the probability of never obtaining a successful split coin, starting with a fresh coin at $x$. This is measurable by [F5] and [F6], lies in $[0,1]$, and satisfies $a=K_0a=Qa-\epsilon1_C\nu(a)$. Integrate against $\pi$ to get $p\nu(a)=0$, hence $\nu(a)=0$. Therefore $a=Qa$ at every state and $a=Q^na$ for all $n$. Convergence of $Q^n(x,\cdot)$ to $\pi$ implies $a(x)=\pi(a)$ for every $x$, since for a measurable $[0,1]$-valued function its expectation difference is bounded by total variation, by integrating level-set indicators. Integrating this constant against $\nu$ makes it zero. Thus every state and every initial law has a finite first success; its post-transition calendar time is an almost surely finite $D\in m\mathbb N$. [F5, F6, F8, step 1.1, step 1.2, given, algebra]

2.2 A skeleton core starts from the $\nu$ endpoint just after a success and includes the successive states through the next successful coin, excluding that successful transition's endpoint. A core of length $\ell$ has probability measure
$$\nu(dx_0)\prod_{i=0}^{\ell-2}K_0(x_i,dx_{i+1})\,\epsilon1_C(x_{\ell-1}).$$
The sum over $\ell\ge1$ has mass one by step 2.1. Its length has the law of $\tau$ in step 1.2: starting in the split atom, one transition draws its initial $\nu$ state, and the next atom visit occurs at precisely that core's inclusive coin count. Hence its length has an exponential moment. Taking iid copies of this core measure supplies all post-success cores; the first state of the next copy supplies the independent $\nu$ endpoint of the preceding successful transition. Multiplying these core kernels reconstructs the split skeleton law. The analogous initial core starts from the given initial law and ends at its first success, before the endpoint drawn from the first iid core. [F5, F6, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct]

3.1 To restore the intermediate states, choose $\rho=\tfrac12\pi+\tfrac12\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-k-1}\mu P^k$ for the given initial law $\mu$. Then $\pi,\mu\ll\rho$ and $\rho P\ll\rho$, by the null-set calculation used directly on this displayed sum. Disintegrate the intermediate word $(X_1,\ldots,X_{m-1})$ conditional on $(X_0,X_m)$ under initial law $\rho$, using [F3]; for $m=1$ take the unique empty word. Denote the kernel by $B(x,y;d\mathbf w)$. Its bridge identity holds for $\rho$-almost every starting point, simultaneously as a probability identity by [F9]. Every starting distribution encountered in a split skeleton is $\rho$-absolutely continuous: $K_0\le Q$ propagates this through failures, and $\nu\ll\pi\ll\rho$ handles successes. Both success and failure endpoint-pair measures are absolutely continuous with respect to $\rho(dx)Q(x,dy)$, because their endpoint kernels are bounded by $Q$. Thus this bridge identity holds on every transition actually sampled. [A1, F3, F6, F8, F9, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct]

3.2 The bridge kernel has a jointly measurable uniform sampler. Code its standard-Borel word space into a Borel subset of $[0,1]$ by [F4]. Its distribution-function evaluations at rational cuts are measurable. The generalized inverse, defined by an infimum over those cuts, is jointly measurable in the endpoints and a uniform variable and has the coded probability law. Its output lies in the coded image almost surely for each endpoint; use a fixed valid word on the Borel complement and decode. For completeness, the word and sequence spaces here are standard Borel: code $S$ into a Borel subset $A\subseteq[0,1]$; $A^{\mathbb N}$ is Borel in the Polish cube by coordinate tests, and finite words are the Borel union of length-marked sequences with fixed trailing coordinates. The extra uniform sequences have the same property. [A1, F3, F4, F6, construct]

3.3 Let $U_j$ consist of the $j$th iid core and an independent infinite sequence of bridge uniforms, using [F5]. For a nonterminal core transition both skeleton endpoints lie in $U_j$. For its terminal successful transition the starting endpoint lies in $U_j$ and the ending endpoint is the first state in $U_{j+1}$; use a uniform in $U_j$ for its bridge. Concatenate each transition's starting state and its $m-1$ intermediate states, excluding its endpoint. This gives a measurable finite word $W(U_j,U_{j+1})$ of length $L(U_j)=m\ell(U_j)$. Concatenate also the finite initial segment from step 2.2, with its terminal bridge ending at the first state's value in $U_0$. Success and failure endpoint kernels add to $Q$, and step 3.1's bridge kernel then restores the original $m$-step path law. Iterating these identities gives the original full $P$-chain law from $\mu$. Thus these words are the claimed delayed calendar tours in a chain copy, with rewards and absolute envelopes measurable functions of two adjacent seeds. [F5, F6, F9, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 3.2, construct]

4.1 The invariant identity is $\pi=\pi K_0+p\nu$. Iteration gives $\pi=p\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\nu K_0^j+\pi K_0^n$. The remainder's total mass is the stationary probability of no successful coin in its first $n$ opportunities, which tends to zero by step 2.1 and monotone convergence. Therefore the potential measure $\eta=\sum_{j\ge0}\nu K_0^j$ equals $\pi/p$. It counts every core state before its fresh coin is sampled, including the state of the terminal successful coin. In particular $\mathbb E\ell=\eta(S)=1/p$ and $\mathbb EL=m/p$. [F6, F8, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.2 For nonnegative measurable $b$, set $c_b(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}P^ib(x)$. The event that a skeleton state is counted in the core is determined before its fresh coin and bridge are sampled. Averaging that coin, its endpoint and bridge makes the conditional expected calendar-block cost $c_b(x)$, because their endpoint mixture is $Q$ and their restored block law is the original one. Hence [F6] and step 4.1 give
$$\mathbb E\sum_{t\text{ in one full tour}}b(X_t)=\eta(c_b)=\frac{\pi(c_b)}p=\frac m p\pi(b)=\mu_L\pi(b).$$
This includes the cost inside the terminal successful bridge. Apply the identity to the positive and negative parts of $f$; $\pi|f|<\infty$ follows from its stated $v$th moment and [F7]. Thus $\mathbb EZ_0=0$. [F6, F7, F8, step 3.1, step 3.3, step 4.1]

4.3 By step 2.2, $\mathbb E\exp(aL)<\infty$ for $a=(\log b)/m>0$. Starting just after a success, the reconstructed infinite chain has initial law $\nu$ and its original $P$-chain marginal, by step 3.3. Since $\pi\ge p\nu$, invariance gives $\mathbb E_\nu|f(X_t)|^v\le\pi(|f|^v)/p$ at every calendar time. For $1\le q<v$, Minkowski and Holder [F7], first on finite sums, imply
$$\left\|\sum_{t=0}^{L-1}|f(X_t)|\right\|_q\le\left(\frac{\pi(|f|^v)}p\right)^{1/v}\sum_{t\ge0}\Pr_\nu(L>t)^{1/q-1/v}<\infty.$$
The exponential length moment makes the series finite; [F6] passes through the increasing finite sums. This proves every claimed spare moment, while $|Z_0|\le H_0$. [F6, F7, F8, step 1.2, step 2.2, step 3.3]

5.1 The constructed state path, its finite delay, and its iid seed sequence have a joint law on standard-Borel spaces by the explicit countable coding in step 3.2. Disintegrate that law conditional on the full state path by [F3], and evaluate the auxiliary kernel at the actual given chain path. Extend its probability space by [F5]. The original entire process is preserved, and its joint law with the seeds and delay is the constructed one. Thus the word equalities, iid seed law, occupation identity and moment conclusions hold on this extension. The initial segment is almost surely finite by step 2.1; since $f$ is finite, its absolute reward is finite, even without an initial-law moment bound. [A1, F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, step 3.2, step 3.3, step 4.2, step 4.3]

5.2 Each length depends only on $U_j$, so the lengths are iid with positive finite mean. Each reward and envelope depends on $(U_j,U_{j+1})$, so their joint sequence with the centered lengths is adjacent-iid, with $\mathbb EZ_0=0$ and all the stated moments. Disjoint seed pairs are independent, giving one-dependence without claiming iid full tours. The same $m,C,\nu$ and core law were selected from $P,\pi,M$, and the single bridge version in step 3.1 uses a $\rho$ dominating both the specified initial law and $\pi$. Thus the same seed law and word functions work from either initial law; only the initial segment and its lifting kernel change. All properties in the Statement follow. The chosen split came from step 1.1 and never used positivity of any supplied one-step minorization, which can therefore be vacuous. [F5, step 3.1, step 3.3, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 4.3, step 5.1] ∎

Assume AC. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on a nonempty standard-Borel space $(S,\mathcal S)$, with invariant probability $\pi$, finite measurable $M:S\to[0,\infty)$ and $0<r<1$ such that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in S,\ n\ge1).$$
Let $f:S\to\mathbb R$ be finite measurable, with $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi(|f|^v)<\infty$ for some $v>1$. For every initial law, on an extension preserving the given chain there are an integer $m\ge1$, an almost surely finite delay $D\in m\mathbb N$, a standard-Borel seed space $E$, iid seeds $(U_j)_{j\ge0}$, and measurable finite-word and length functions $W:E^2\to\bigsqcup_{k\ge1}S^k$ and $L:E\to m\mathbb N$ with the following properties.

Put $T_0=D$ and $T_{j+1}=T_j+L(U_j)$. Almost surely, simultaneously for all $j\ge0$,
$$\bigl(X_{T_j},\ldots,X_{T_{j+1}-1}\bigr)=W(U_j,U_{j+1}).$$
Write $L_j=L(U_j)$, $Z_j=\sum_{t=T_j}^{T_{j+1}-1}f(X_t)$, and $H_j=\sum_{t=T_j}^{T_{j+1}-1}|f(X_t)|$. Then $Z_j=z(U_j,U_{j+1})$ and $H_j=h(U_j,U_{j+1})$ for measurable functions $z,h$, and
$$\mathbb E e^{aL_0}<\infty\text{ for some }a>0,\qquad 0<\mu_L:=\mathbb EL_0<\infty,$$
$$\mathbb EZ_0=0,\qquad \mathbb EH_0^q<\infty\quad(1\le q<v).$$

$$\mathbb E\sum_{t=T_0}^{T_1-1}b(X_t)=\mu_L\pi(b).$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be a countably generated measurable space ([[def-measurable-space]]), $P$ a probability kernel ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and $\phi$ a nonzero $\sigma$-finite measure ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) on $\mathcal X$. Write $P^n$ for the $n$-fold kernel iterate. The kernel is **$\phi$-irreducible** if, for every $A\in\mathcal X$ with $\phi(A)>0$ and every $x\in\mathsf X$, there is an integer $n\ge1$ such that $P^n(x,A)>0$. Equivalently, the sum of these nonnegative probabilities over $n\ge1$ is positive. No recurrence or invariant law is part of this definition.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be countably generated, let $P$ be a probability kernel, and let $\phi$ be a nonzero $\sigma$-finite irreducibility measure. Then there are an integer $m\ge1$, a measurable $C$ with $\phi(C)>0$, a probability $
u$ with $
u(C)>0$, and $\epsilon>0$ such that $P^m(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon
u(\cdot)$ for every $x\in C$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $Q$ be a probability kernel on any measurable space $(X,\mathcal G)$, with invariant probability $\pi$. Let $C\in\mathcal G$ satisfy $\pi(C)>0$, and suppose
$$Q(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon\nu(\cdot)\quad(x\in C),\qquad 0<\epsilon<1,$$
where $\nu$ is a probability measure. Suppose some $A<\infty$ and $0<\theta<1$ satisfy
$$|\nu Q^n(C)-\pi(C)|\le A\theta^n\quad(n\ge0).$$
For a $Q$-chain started at $x$, put $\sigma_C=\inf\{n\ge0:X_n\in C\}$. Then some $s>1$ makes
$$H(x)=\mathbb E_x[s^{\sigma_C}]\quad\text{measurable},\qquad \pi(H)<\infty,$$
where $s^\infty=\infty$. In particular $H$ is finite $\pi$-almost everywhere; finiteness at every state is not asserted.

For the same hypotheses, the split construction also has the following return and occupation properties. Put $w_1(x)=\epsilon1_C(x)$ and $w_0(x)=1-w_1(x)$. Define $K_{x,1}=\nu$, $K_{x,0}=(Q(x,\cdot)-\epsilon\nu)/(1-\epsilon)$ on $C$, and $K_{x,0}=Q(x,\cdot)$ off $C$. On $X\times\{0,1\}$ use the kernel
$$\widetilde Q((x,i),dy\times\{j\})=K_{x,i}(dy)w_j(y)$$
and invariant law $\widetilde\pi(dx,i)=w_i(x)\pi(dx)$. Its atom $\alpha=C\times\{1\}$ has mass $p=\epsilon\pi(C)>0$. If $Z_0$ has law $\kappa=\widetilde\pi(\cdot\mid\alpha)$ and $\tau=\inf\{n\ge1:Z_n\in\alpha\}$, then some $b>1$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E_\kappa b^\tau<\infty,$$
and for every nonnegative measurable $g$ on the split space,
$$\widetilde\pi(g)=p\,\mathbb E_\kappa\sum_{k=0}^{\tau-1}g(Z_k).$$
In particular $\tau<\infty$ almost surely and $\mathbb E_\kappa\tau=1/p$. These additional assertions use exactly the construction and hypotheses above; they do not assert an exponential entrance-time moment from every state.

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.
Assume AC. Every standard-Borel space $(E,\mathcal S)$ is measurably isomorphic to a Borel subset of $[0,1]$, including $E=\varnothing$.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. A countable product of Polish spaces is Polish, and every $G_\delta$ subspace of a Polish space is Polish.

Assume Choice. For every probability measure $\mu$ and probability kernel $K$
on an arbitrary measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, the canonical path space
$$ (E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}) $$
carries a unique probability $\mathbb P_\mu$ under which the coordinate maps
form a Markov chain with initial law $\mu$ and transition kernel $K$.

Assume countable choice and dependent choice. For probability spaces
$(E_n,\mathcal E_n,\mu_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ there is a unique probability measure
$\mu$ on $\mathcal C_{\mathbb N}$ such that, for every finite $F$, its
$F$-coordinate marginal is $\bigotimes_{n\in F}\mu_n$.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f,g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p.$$
2. If $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty.$$

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be countably generated, let $P$ be a probability kernel, and let $\phi$ be a nonzero $\sigma$-finite irreducibility measure. Then there are an integer $m\ge1$, a measurable $C$ with $\phi(C)>0$, a probability $
u$ with $
u(C)>0$, and $\epsilon>0$ such that $P^m(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon
u(\cdot)$ for every $x\in C$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $Q$ be a probability kernel on any measurable space $(X,\mathcal G)$, with invariant probability $\pi$. Let $C\in\mathcal G$ satisfy $\pi(C)>0$, and suppose
$$Q(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon\nu(\cdot)\quad(x\in C),\qquad 0<\epsilon<1,$$
where $\nu$ is a probability measure. Suppose some $A<\infty$ and $0<\theta<1$ satisfy
$$|\nu Q^n(C)-\pi(C)|\le A\theta^n\quad(n\ge0).$$
For a $Q$-chain started at $x$, put $\sigma_C=\inf\{n\ge0:X_n\in C\}$. Then some $s>1$ makes
$$H(x)=\mathbb E_x[s^{\sigma_C}]\quad\text{measurable},\qquad \pi(H)<\infty,$$
where $s^\infty=\infty$. In particular $H$ is finite $\pi$-almost everywhere; finiteness at every state is not asserted.

For the same hypotheses, the split construction also has the following return and occupation properties. Put $w_1(x)=\epsilon1_C(x)$ and $w_0(x)=1-w_1(x)$. Define $K_{x,1}=\nu$, $K_{x,0}=(Q(x,\cdot)-\epsilon\nu)/(1-\epsilon)$ on $C$, and $K_{x,0}=Q(x,\cdot)$ off $C$. On $X\times\{0,1\}$ use the kernel
$$\widetilde Q((x,i),dy\times\{j\})=K_{x,i}(dy)w_j(y)$$
and invariant law $\widetilde\pi(dx,i)=w_i(x)\pi(dx)$. Its atom $\alpha=C\times\{1\}$ has mass $p=\epsilon\pi(C)>0$. If $Z_0$ has law $\kappa=\widetilde\pi(\cdot\mid\alpha)$ and $\tau=\inf\{n\ge1:Z_n\in\alpha\}$, then some $b>1$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E_\kappa b^\tau<\infty,$$
and for every nonnegative measurable $g$ on the split space,
$$\widetilde\pi(g)=p\,\mathbb E_\kappa\sum_{k=0}^{\tau-1}g(Z_k).$$

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.
Assume AC. Every standard-Borel space $(E,\mathcal S)$ is measurably isomorphic to a Borel subset of $[0,1]$, including $E=\varnothing$.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. A countable product of Polish spaces is Polish, and every $G_\delta$ subspace of a Polish space is Polish.

Assume Choice. For every probability measure $\mu$ and probability kernel $K$
on an arbitrary measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, the canonical path space
$$ (E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}) $$
carries a unique probability $\mathbb P_\mu$ under which the coordinate maps
form a Markov chain with initial law $\mu$ and transition kernel $K$.

Assume countable choice and dependent choice. For probability spaces
$(E_n,\mathcal E_n,\mu_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ there is a unique probability measure
$\mu$ on $\mathcal C_{\mathbb N}$ such that, for every finite $F$, its
$F$-coordinate marginal is $\bigotimes_{n\in F}\mu_n$.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f,g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p.$$
2. If $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty.$$

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

kernel $I(x,A)=1_A(x)$ and define

space. Induction using the published kernel-composition lemma shows that every

$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

manifest_rows.title: A geometrically ergodic chain has an all-start standard-Borel observation factor
manifest_rows.statement:
Assume AC. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on an arbitrary measurable space $(X,\mathcal F)$, with invariant probability $\pi$, finite measurable $M:X\to[0,\infty)$ and $0<r<1$ satisfying
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in X,\ n\ge1).$$
Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be finite measurable. For each specified initial law $\mu$, there are a nonempty standard-Borel space $S$, a probability kernel $T$ on $S$, an invariant probability $\widehat\pi$, an initial probability $\widehat\mu$, and finite measurable functions $\varphi:S\to\mathbb R$ and $\widehat M:S\to[0,\infty)$ such that
$$\|T^n(z,\cdot)-\widehat\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\widehat M(z)r^n\quad(z\in S,\ n\ge1).$$
The complete observation path $(f(X_n))_{n\ge0}$ of a $\mu$-started $P$-chain has the same law as $(\varphi(Y_n))_{n\ge0}$ of a $\widehat\mu$-started $T$-chain. The corresponding stationary observation paths also have the same law, and $\widehat\pi(|\varphi|^a)=\pi(|f|^a)$ for every $a>0$, with infinity allowed. The factor may depend on $\mu$.

Moreover, any joint law of that observation path with a random element of a standard-Borel space can be lifted to an extension preserving the entire original chain probability space and process.

manifest_rows.title: Geometric Markov chains admit delayed adjacent-iid split tours with spare moments
manifest_rows.statement:
Assume AC. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on a nonempty standard-Borel space $(S,\mathcal S)$, with invariant probability $\pi$, finite measurable $M:S\to[0,\infty)$ and $0<r<1$ such that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in S,\ n\ge1).$$
Let $f:S\to\mathbb R$ be finite measurable, with $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi(|f|^v)<\infty$ for some $v>1$. For every initial law, on an extension preserving the given chain there are an integer $m\ge1$, an almost surely finite delay $D\in m\mathbb N$, a standard-Borel seed space $E$, iid seeds $(U_j)_{j\ge0}$, and measurable finite-word and length functions $W:E^2\to\bigsqcup_{k\ge1}S^k$ and $L:E\to m\mathbb N$ with the following properties.

Put $T_0=D$ and $T_{j+1}=T_j+L(U_j)$. Almost surely, simultaneously for all $j\ge0$,
$$\bigl(X_{T_j},\ldots,X_{T_{j+1}-1}\bigr)=W(U_j,U_{j+1}).$$
Write $L_j=L(U_j)$, $Z_j=\sum_{t=T_j}^{T_{j+1}-1}f(X_t)$, and $H_j=\sum_{t=T_j}^{T_{j+1}-1}|f(X_t)|$. Then $Z_j=z(U_j,U_{j+1})$ and $H_j=h(U_j,U_{j+1})$ for measurable functions $z,h$, and
$$\mathbb E e^{aL_0}<\infty\text{ for some }a>0,\qquad 0<\mu_L:=\mathbb EL_0<\infty,$$
$$\mathbb EZ_0=0,\qquad \mathbb EH_0^q<\infty\quad(1\le q<v).$$
For every nonnegative measurable $b:S\to[0,\infty]$ the full-tour occupation identity is
$$\mathbb E\sum_{t=T_0}^{T_1-1}b(X_t)=\mu_L\pi(b).$$
For each specified initial law, the same $m$, iid seed law, $W,L$ and post-delay tour law can be used also for the invariant initial law $\pi$; only the finite initial segment and coupling change.

In particular $(L_j-\mu_L,Z_j)$ is an adjacent-iid centered vector sequence, while the lengths themselves are iid. Full tour words or rewards are not asserted to be iid. No moment of $D$ or of the initial finite prefix is required, and the construction uses a useful multistep split chosen from $P$ rather than requiring any supplied one-step minorization to have positive stationary mass.
